newsitem.title: UK: Dollar bulls play cat and mouse with central banks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar bulls play cat and mouse with central banks.

text.p: Foreign exchange traders have shrugged aside yet another bout of G7 rhetoric aimed at stemming the dollar's rise, and will test the central banks' resolve by bidding the dollar up gradually, analysts said.

"For this week at least the forex market will be a bit nervous but assuming no intervention comes through I think we will be back to seeing people becoming reasonably bullish on the dollar again," said Stephen King, International Economist at HSBC James Capel.
The weekend Group of Seven (G7) meeting in Washington emphasised the importance of avoiding exchange rates that could lead to the re-emergence of large external imbalances.
In February, the Berlin G7 meeting said that "Major misalignments in exchange markets had been corrected."

Despite newspaper headlines proclaiming that G7 officials had called for action on the strong dollar the difference between the Berlin and Washington statements was too subtle to have much impact on the average investor, analysts said.
"The market will continue to gradually test the upside and watch for official reaction in the way of intervention," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
"If none is forthcoming the market will play cat and mouse with the central banks and keep pushing the dollar higher."

Analysts said given that the dollar has risen another four percent on the mark and three percent on the yen between the Berlin and Washington meetings, it was more a case of what was not said in Washington rather than what was said.
Forex traders say continued verbal intervention will have little or no impact and only a dose of actual central bank dollar selling will calm the dollar bulls down.

"Jawboning isn't enough, only intervention will stop it in the short-term," said one trader at a leading U.S. bank. "And there is a big enough question mark over possible intervention to keep the dollar bulls happy."

Even though the Washington communique said G7 would "...cooperate as appropriate in foreign exchange markets" traders still reckon that the United States and Europe are fairly relaxed about the dollar's strength simply because it helps the U.S. inflation outlook and European growth.
If this is true it leaves Japan out on a limb and unilateral intervention by the Bank of Japan would only have limited success, analysts said.
"It remains to be seen whether the co-operation G7 talks about will extend to intervention in the currency market," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.
"We suspect that it has been harder to reach an agreement on this issue, the Bundesbank is probably wary of ineffective intervention."
Dollar sentiment will change when the market changes its view for the prospects for the Japanese, U.S. and European economies, and that could be some way off.
Until the economic outlook changes and the interest rate differential that the dollar is enjoying starts to be eroded it will be extremely hard to rein it in, analysts said.
